lesson.title: Marching for What Was Promised: The Bonus Army of 1932
lesson.summary: In the summer of 1932, thousands of desperate World War I veterans marched on Washington to demand early payment of a bonus they had been promised, only to be violently driven out by the United States Army, a turning point in public opinion against Hoover.
lesson.body:
Many of the men struggling through the Depression's worst years were veterans of World War I, having served under the wartime draft established by the Selective Service Act. In 1924, Congress had promised these veterans a bonus in the form of certificates, but the payment was not due to be paid out until 1945. With the Depression leaving so many veterans unemployed and desperate, pressure built to demand that Congress pay the bonus immediately rather than waiting more than two decades.

In the summer of 1932, an estimated fifteen to twenty thousand veterans, many bringing wives and children, traveled to Washington, D.C., and set up encampments around the city, the largest at Anacostia Flats. They called themselves the Bonus Expeditionary Force, deliberately echoing the name of the wartime American Expeditionary Forces they had served in. Congress considered a bill, often called the Patman Bill after its sponsor, to pay the bonus early. The House of Representatives passed it, but the Senate rejected it in mid-June 1932, a bitter disappointment that led many veterans to remain camped in the capital in protest.

Late in July 1932, Hoover ordered the Army to clear veterans who had occupied several downtown federal buildings. General Douglas MacArthur led the operation, with junior officers Dwight Eisenhower and George Patton also involved. The action went well beyond simply clearing the buildings: troops used tanks, bayonets, and tear gas, and pushed on to the main encampment at Anacostia Flats, which was burned in the process.

The public reaction was one of shock and outrage at the sight of the United States Army using force against its own veterans and their families. News coverage and photographs of the eviction badly damaged Hoover's already weakened standing with the public, reinforcing the image, already forming around Hoovervilles and his limited relief efforts, of a president out of touch with the suffering of ordinary Americans. The Bonus Army episode became one of the defining low points of Hoover's presidency and helped set the stage for his landslide defeat that November by Franklin D. Roosevelt.
